why: Identical to cad-0117 (vasospastic angina treated with a calcium-channel blocker)

set.explanation: An inferior STEMI with hypotension, cool peripheries, pulmonary crackles and a raised JVP is complicated by cardiogenic shock, and emergency revascularisation of the culprit artery by PCI is the only intervention shown to improve survival (SHOCK trial). Nitrates and IV beta-blockers would worsen the hypotension, a single antiplatelet drug alone is inadequate, and CABG is only for anatomy unsuitable for PCI or mechanical complications.

why: Same idea as cad-0043 (post-MI ventricular septal rupture)
Same idea as cad-0108 (unstable angina: admit and anticoagulate)

set.stem: A 42-year-old man who smokes has sudden crushing central chest pain, nausea, sweating and breathlessness; the ECG shows anteroseptal ST elevation but cardiac enzymes stay normal. Emergency angiography shows only a 25% LAD stenosis and no intervention is performed. Which treatment would most reduce the risk of further episodes?
set.explanation: Transient ST elevation without infarction and with near-normal coronary arteries suggests coronary vasospasm. Calcium-channel blockers (diltiazem or nifedipine), with nitrates and complete smoking cessation, prevent attacks. A 25% stenosis does not need a stent, ACE inhibitors do not prevent spasm, and non-selective beta-blockers may make spasm worse by leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed.

set.stem: A 55-year-old man admitted with chest pain has normal cardiac enzymes, BP 140/90–150/100 mmHg, a soft early systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge, and a resting ECG showing left ventricular hypertrophy with secondary ST–T changes. Why is an exercise ECG not an appropriate test for him?
set.explanation: Resting ST–T abnormalities (LVH with strain, LBBB, digoxin effect, WPW, paced rhythm) make exercise-induced ST depression uninterpretable, so a functional imaging test (stress echo, perfusion scintigraphy or MRI) or CT coronary angiography is used instead. Mild hypertension, an innocent-sounding flow murmur and anxiety do not contraindicate testing; only severe symptomatic aortic stenosis or unstable angina would.

options: Admit to a monitored bed and repeat enzymes and ECG in 6 hours without further treatment
Load a P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel 300–600 mg or ticagrelor 180 mg)
set.explanation: This is an NSTEMI (raised troponin, T-wave inversion) in a stable patient who has had aspirin, nitrate and LMWH; the missing class I therapy is a P2Y12 inhibitor loading dose to complete dual antiplatelet therapy, followed by angiography within 24 hours. Thrombolysis is harmful without ST elevation, emergency catheterisation is for very high-risk features, and there is no heart failure to need a diuretic.

why: Original key (IV beta-blocker) is not current first-line practice and the clopidogrel option had a wrong dosing schedule; options rewritten and key changed to P2Y12 loading

set.explanation: The ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in aVL, which is an acute inferior STEMI; the preceding exertional pain was angina. Pericarditis gives widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal change, and costochondritis or reflux do not cause ST elevation. A family history of gallstones is a distractor.

Claudication with an ABPI of 0.6 is managed first with risk-factor control (stopping smoking, a statin, antiplatelet therapy, blood pressure and diabetes control) and a supervised exercise programme; cilostazol or naftidrofuryl can be added if exercise alone is not enough. Warfarin does not help, and angiography or surgical referral is reserved for lifestyle-limiting symptoms despite this, or for critical limb ischaemia.

options: Aspirin, calcium-channel blocker, morphine and primary PCI
Aspirin, ticagrelor, heparin and primary PCI
Aspirin and IV thrombolysis after 3 hours of observation
set.explanation: The ECG shows an anterior STEMI within an hour of onset. Management is aspirin plus a potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel), anticoagulation and immediate primary PCI. Opioids are used only for severe pain, beta-blockers are started orally once the patient is stable rather than routinely IV, calcium-channel blockers have no benefit, and any strategy without prompt reperfusion is inadequate.

why: Original options had two defensible answers and no P2Y12 inhibitor; rewritten to reflect current STEMI management
Same idea as cad-0098 (cardiac syndrome X)

set.explanation: In ACS, hyperglycaemia above 11 mmol/L should be managed with a dose-adjusted IV insulin infusion, avoiding hypoglycaemia (NICE CG130). Metformin is withheld around contrast angiography and in cardiogenic shock (risk of lactic acidosis), and sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and are hard to titrate acutely. Oral therapy or a subcutaneous insulin regimen is resumed once he is eating and stable.

Bradycardia and hypotension with chest pain suggest an inferior MI with involvement of the AV node or right ventricle, both supplied by the right coronary artery in most people (the AV nodal artery arises from the dominant RCA). AV block in inferior MI is usually nodal and transient and responds to atropine, whereas heart block with an anterior (LAD) infarct means extensive septal damage and a worse prognosis.

ST elevation in I and aVL is a high lateral infarct (circumflex or first diagonal branch); if V5 and V6 are also involved it is described as lateral. Anteroseptal changes are in V1–V4 (LAD), extensive anterior (anterolateral) changes involve V1–V6 with I and aVL (proximal LAD), inferior changes in II, III and aVF, and posterior infarction shows as ST depression in V1–V3.

why: Same idea as cad-0084 (cholesterol embolisation after angiography)

set.explanation: NICE CG95 (2016 update) recommends 64-slice CT coronary angiography as the first-line test for typical or atypical angina, or non-anginal pain with an abnormal ECG. Functional non-invasive imaging is used if CTCA is non-diagnostic, and invasive angiography if the results suggest the need for revascularisation. The exercise ECG is no longer recommended for diagnosis because of its poor sensitivity.

Troponin stays raised for 7–14 days after an MI, so a second rise is hard to interpret early on, whereas CK-MB normalises within 2–3 days and a fresh rise indicates reinfarction. With high-sensitivity troponin, a further rise of more than 20% from a stable or falling baseline is also used. LDH and AST are non-specific.

set.stem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with aortic dissection?
set.explanation: Bicuspid aortic valve is associated with aortopathy (medial degeneration) and carries a raised risk of ascending aortic dilatation and dissection. Other predisposing conditions are hypertension (the commonest), Marfan, Loeys–Dietz and vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndromes, coarctation, Turner syndrome, pregnancy and cocaine. Acromegaly and sarcoidosis are not recognised associations.

why: Same idea as cad-0132 (tearing chest pain to the back in hypertension = aortic dissection)

set.explanation: Sudden, severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back in a hypertensive patient, with a pulse deficit or blood-pressure difference between the arms, is aortic dissection until proved otherwise; other clues are aortic regurgitation, a widened mediastinum and neurological deficits. MI causes crushing pain without pulse deficits, pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic pain and hypoxia, and oesophageal rupture follows vomiting.

CT angiography of the whole aorta is the first-line confirmatory test in a stable patient: it is fast, widely available and shows the intimal flap, its extent and branch involvement. Transoesophageal echo is used in unstable patients or theatre; transthoracic echo and chest X-ray are too insensitive to exclude dissection. A normal D-dimer makes dissection less likely but cannot confirm it.

Stanford type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and carries a mortality of about 1–2% per hour untreated from rupture, tamponade, acute aortic regurgitation or coronary occlusion. It needs emergency surgical repair once heart rate and blood pressure are controlled with IV beta-blockers. Type B (descending) dissection is usually treated medically, with endovascular stenting for complications, and thrombolysis or anticoagulation is dangerous.

Proximal dissection can rupture into the pericardium, causing haemopericardium and tamponade, which is a leading cause of death; it can also cause acute aortic regurgitation, coronary (usually right) occlusion and branch-vessel ischaemia (stroke, limb, renal or mesenteric). Pericardiocentesis alone may worsen bleeding, so these patients go straight to surgery.

When a hypertensive patient has sudden severe chest pain and the ECG and troponin do not show MI, aortic dissection must be actively excluded, because antiplatelet drugs, anticoagulants or thrombolysis given for a presumed ACS can cause fatal bleeding. Pneumothorax, pericarditis and myocarditis usually have other clues, and anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion.

An early diastolic murmur is caused by aortic (or pulmonary) regurgitation. In Marfan syndrome, dilatation of the aortic root stretches the valve ring and causes aortic regurgitation, alongside the risk of dissection. Mitral valve prolapse causes a mid-systolic click and a late systolic murmur, and long QT, WPW and myotonic dystrophy are electrical or conduction disorders.

Diabetes is consistently associated with a lower prevalence and slower growth of abdominal aortic aneurysms, possibly because glycation stiffens and cross-links the aortic wall matrix. Smoking is the strongest risk factor (and speeds expansion); others are male sex, age, family history, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia.

Continued smoking increases the rate of AAA growth and rupture risk, and stopping smoking is the most effective modifiable intervention. Blood pressure control and a statin reduce overall cardiovascular risk, but ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and statins have not convincingly slowed aneurysm growth in trials, and anticoagulation has no role.

why: Same idea as cad-0134 (type A dissection needs emergency surgery)

set.explanation: Pregnancy is a recognised risk factor for aortic dissection, usually in the third trimester or peripartum, because of hormonal changes in the aortic media and the increased cardiac output and blood volume. Half of pregnancy-related dissections occur in women with Marfan syndrome, but this short woman had no marfanoid features and was normotensive, so pregnancy itself is the most likely precipitant.

Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in FBN1, which encodes fibrillin-1, a structural component of elastic microfibrils; this leads to excess TGF-beta signalling. Features include tall stature with long limbs, lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), aortic root dilatation with aortic regurgitation and dissection, and mitral valve prolapse. Myosin, myosin-binding protein and troponin mutations cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and titin mutations cause dilated cardiomyopathy.

set.stem: Four days after an open aortobifemoral bypass, a CT scan shows a pseudoaneurysm just proximal to the aortic origin of the graft. Which of the following best defines a pseudoaneurysm?
set.explanation: A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the arterial wall. A pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm) is a contained rupture: the intima and media are breached and the blood is held only by adventitia or surrounding tissue, often after arterial puncture, surgery or trauma. A dilatation involving only part of the circumference is a saccular aneurysm.

Degenerative aortic aneurysms are several times more common in men; female sex is not a risk factor, although aneurysms in women rupture at smaller diameters. Age, smoking, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, atherosclerosis and family history all increase the risk.

Aortic root aneurysm in a young man with hypertelorism, a bifid or broad uvula and a family history of arterial aneurysms and sudden death suggests Loeys–Dietz syndrome, caused by mutations in the TGF-beta receptor genes (TGFBR1/2, also SMAD3). Aneurysms dissect at smaller diameters and are widespread, so repair is recommended earlier than in Marfan syndrome (FBN1). Type III procollagen (COL3A1) mutations cause vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome.

Uncomplicated type B dissection, confined to the descending aorta beyond the left subclavian artery, is managed medically with IV beta-blockade and blood-pressure control. Surgery or endovascular repair is reserved for complications: rupture, malperfusion (renal, mesenteric or limb), rapid expansion or refractory pain, as in the dissection involving both renal arteries. Any involvement of the ascending aorta or root, including an intramural haematoma there, is treated as type A and needs surgery.

set.stem: An incidental CT finding in a 32-year-old woman is dilatation of the ascending aorta to 4.3 cm. All of the following are recognised causes of this finding EXCEPT:
set.explanation: Inflammatory causes of ascending aortic dilatation include giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, tertiary syphilis (aortitis with 'tree-bark' intima), and seronegative and rheumatoid arthritis. Other causes are connective-tissue disorders (Marfan, Loeys–Dietz, Ehlers–Danlos), bicuspid aortic valve and degenerative disease. SLE is not a recognised cause of aortic dilatation.

why: Same idea as cad-0132 (sudden severe chest pain to the back = aortic dissection)
Same idea as cad-0132 (tearing chest pain to the back = aortic dissection)

set.explanation: A 3.0–3.5 cm AAA is small: it is monitored with ultrasound (roughly yearly for 3.0–4.4 cm, every 3 months for 4.5–5.4 cm) while risk factors are treated. Repair is considered at 5.5 cm or more, with growth of more than 1 cm a year, or with symptoms. Endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) is an established alternative to open surgery, and renal artery involvement affects the technique rather than the indication.

Tearing pain to the back, severe hypertension, new aortic regurgitation and a widened mediastinum indicate proximal aortic dissection, with pulmonary oedema from acute AR. Initial management is an IV beta-blocker to lower heart rate and shear stress, then a vasodilator such as nitroprusside, and rapid imaging (TOE or CT) before emergency surgery. Heparin, PCI or diuresis and digoxin would be inappropriate or dangerous.

A one-off abdominal ultrasound to screen for AAA is recommended for men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked (USPSTF), and in the UK all men are invited at 65, because screening reduces aneurysm-related deaths. Carotid ultrasound, exercise testing, Lp(a) and homocysteine are not recommended for screening asymptomatic adults.
